n: When the enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard the returnees were rebuilding the temple, they took notice. Every good work tends to draw opposition.

They approached Zerubbabel and offered to help, claiming to worship the same God since Assyria’s king Esarhaddon resettled them there. They were descendants of foreigners mixed with Israelites, whose worship combined the Lord with other gods.

f.g: King of Assyria about 681–669 BC, son of Sennacherib.

f.w: we seek your God, as ye do

n: Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the leaders refused: you have no part with us; we alone will build, as Cyrus commanded. They protected the purity of worship from mixed religion.

f.w: Ye have nothing to do with us

n: Rebuffed, the local people discouraged and frightened the builders. “Weakened the hands” means to demoralize.

f.g: Discouraged; sapped their resolve.
Here, the non-exiled, mixed population surrounding Judah.

n: They even bribed Persian officials to block the project from Cyrus’s reign until Darius’s reign — about sixteen years of delay.

f.g: Bribed advisers or officials.
Darius I, who reigned 522–486 BC.

n: Ezra now jumps ahead to show this opposition continued for generations: under Ahasuerus (Xerxes, 486–465 BC) they filed an accusation against Judah. This is the same king as in the book of Esther.

f.g: Xerxes I, king of Persia.

n: Later still, under Artaxerxes (465–424 BC), officials wrote another letter in Aramaic. From here to Ezra 6:18 the original text is in Aramaic, the international language of the Persian Empire.

f.g: Aramaic — the diplomatic language of the empire; Ezra 4:8–6:18 is written in Aramaic.
Artaxerxes I, who later sent Ezra and Nehemiah.

n: Rehum the commanding officer and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes. These verses (8–23) concern rebuilding the city walls, not the temple — placed here to show a pattern of opposition.

f.g: Commanding officer or governor; literally ‘master of decree.’

n: The letter came from Rehum, Shimshai, and their colleagues representing peoples resettled from many places — judges, officials, and people from Erech, Babylon, Susa, and Elam.

f.g: People from Susa (Shushan), a Persian capital.
People from Erech (Uruk) in Babylonia.

n: These were nations the great Osnappar (probably the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal) had deported to Samaria and the province “beyond the River.”

f.g: Probably Ashurbanipal, king of Assyria (about 668–627 BC).
West of the Euphrates — the Persian province called ‘Beyond the River.’
‘And so forth’ — a letter formula, like ‘etc.’

n: The copy of the letter begins with a standard greeting from the king’s servants in the province beyond the River.
The accusation: the Jews who came from you are rebuilding that rebellious, wicked city, finishing the walls and repairing the foundations.

f.w: the rebellious and the bad city

n: If the city is rebuilt, they will stop paying taxes, tolls, and duties, and the royal treasury will suffer. The enemies appealed to the king’s self-interest.

f.g: Different kinds of taxes: tribute, poll tax, and land tax or tolls.
Damage; harm.

n: “Because we eat the king’s salt, it isn’t right for us to see him dishonored” — so we’re informing the king. They posed as loyal servants.

f.w: we have maintenance from the king's palace
f.g: Literally ‘we eat the salt of the palace’ — an idiom for being bound in loyalty to the king.
Fitting; proper.

n: They urged the king to check the royal archives, where he would find that Jerusalem had a long history of rebellion — the very reason it was destroyed. Half-truths can be powerful weapons.

f.g: Rebellion against authority.

n: If the city and walls are rebuilt, you will lose control of the whole province west of the Euphrates — an exaggerated threat.

f.g: No share or possession.

n: The king replied to Rehum, Shimshai, and their colleagues in Samaria and beyond the River with greetings.

f.g: A standard letter greeting (Aramaic shelam).

n: Artaxerxes said the letter had been translated and read clearly before him.

f.g: Read clearly, or translated and read.

n: A search of the records confirmed that Jerusalem had revolted against kings in the past.
The records also showed powerful kings had once ruled from Jerusalem over the whole region and collected tribute — a reminder of David and Solomon’s empire.
So the king ordered the work stopped until he himself gave further orders — leaving the door open, which later allowed Nehemiah’s mission.

f.w: until another commandment shall be given from me

n: Be careful to carry this out — why let harm grow against the king’s interests?
As soon as the letter was read, Rehum, Shimshai, and their associates hurried to Jerusalem and forced the Jews to stop by armed force.

f.g: By force of arms.

n: Returning to the temple story (resuming from verse 5): the work on God’s house stopped until Darius’s second year (520 BC) — about sixteen years of silence. But God was about to raise up prophets.

f.w: the second year of the reign of Darius
